Parler de menstruations n’est pas quelqu: Talking about menstruation isn’t very common, either in the culture I come from or among people of my generation. A friend who has an 11-year-old daughter told me that some young girls hold a kind of ceremony when they get their first period. That made me happy, because I’ve always felt it was high time for new generations to go through this natural process with more openness and fewer taboos.
En parlant avec une autre amie, j’ai déc: While talking with another friend, I discovered the workshops of Diana Palacios, a Colombian woman based in Montréal who launched her project, Happy Periods, in 2021. She takes a very holistic approach to encouraging a better understanding of the menstrual cycle, particularly as an indicator of women’s health. That was when I decided to do this story and dive into the world of menstruation: a cycle that can reconnect women with their bodies and their inner rhythm.
J’ai voulu comprendre comment ce sujet e: I wanted to understand how this subject is perceived in Quebec today, especially since I’m leaving this phase of my life myself and entering another: menopause. A stage that is also covered in this story.
En discutant avec Diana Palacios et troi: In speaking with Diana Palacios and three other Latin American women, and in reviewing United Nations data, I realized that taboos around menstruation are still very much present, as are stigma and a lack of understanding of menstrual health.
Aujourd’hui est soulignée la Journée mon: Today is World Menstrual Hygiene Day. What better time to break the silence?
Mi-mai, dans une petite salle d’un café: Mid-May, in a small room of a café in the McGill Ghetto in Montréal. Three women have gathered for an interview and an intimate discussion about menstruation. Spring has settled in, and the sun is gently warming the city. Talking about hot flashes comes like a much-needed breath of air, right on time.
L’une des femmes, Yusle Rodríguez, est m: One of the women, Yusle Rodríguez, is a mother and is accompanied by her eight-year-old daughter, who has already taken part in workshops on the menstrual cycle. Another, Claudia Gamboa, has no children. She is well into her thirties and has brought her closest friends together in this café, which she owns, for an information workshop on menstruation.
La troisième, Diana Palacios, est celle: The third, Diana Palacios, is the one sharing the knowledge: she gives workshops on menstruation and on the “power of the feminine.” While the other two women share their experiences, she listens, clarifies and informs.
Originaire de Colombie, Diana dit être t: Originally from Colombia, Diana says she fell in love with Montréal, a city she first came to know while pursuing a master’s degree… and where she stayed, in fact, for love.
Son cheminement vers l’activisme a comme: Her path to activism began with a menstrual cup. “It changed my life. I reconnected with my body, with my blood, and I started collecting my menstrual blood to use in the soil, as a natural fertilizer. It was a way of making peace with my body.”
Cette transformation personnelle l’a ame: That personal transformation led her to train as an educator at the Emancipadas menstrual education school in Medellín, and to found the Happy Periods project in 2021.
Dans le cadre de cette initiative, et pa: Through this initiative, and by way of “positive, healthy and lasting” experiences, she aims to give the menstrual cycle and periods a new meaning for girls, teens and women. Young girls can, for example, draw the uterus, read stories, draw the body and its changes, or play card games in which they match pairs of the different parts of the female reproductive system.
L’éducation menstruelle est également un: Menstrual education is also a way of addressing other subjects close to her heart: environmental education, social responsibility, community change and the valuing of local products.
« De quelle couleur est ton sang menstru: “What colour is your menstrual blood?” It’s the question she often uses to start her workshops. The usual answer? Silence. Some participants shrug, others look down.
« Beaucoup de femmes arrivent à mes atel: “Many women come to my workshops at 30 or 40 without knowing how their cycle works. Nobody ever talked to them about their body, their blood, their uterus,” she laments. The menstrual cycle is nevertheless an important indicator of women’s health, she adds, and it should be recognized as such.
« Avoir ses règles, c’est un signe vital: “Getting your period is a vital sign of health. If I get it regularly, it means my body is working well, and that deserves to be celebrated,” she insists.

L’expérience menstruelle a longtemps été: The menstrual experience has long been marked by taboo, shame and silence, which also explains the widespread misinformation. And it’s no different from one country to another. Diana observes that this phenomenon repeats itself even in so-called more open societies, like Canada.
« Le tabou est partout. Je l’ai vécu en: “The taboo is everywhere. I experienced it in Colombia and I see it here in Quebec. It doesn’t matter whether she’s a Latina, African or Asian woman… the silence always returns,” she says.
Au Québec, une <l1>étude rendue publique: In Quebec, a <l1>study made public in 2023</l1> by the Réseau québécois d’action pour la santé des femmes (RQASF) found that the devaluing of periods remains very present in everyday life. Two-thirds of respondents (65%) said they had been stigmatized, ridiculed or criticized in connection with their periods.
De plus en plus de voix cherchent à rend: More and more voices are seeking to make this silence and stigma visible, and to transform them.
C’est l’un des objectifs de la Journée m: That is one of the goals of World Menstrual Hygiene Day. The meaning of the date is simple and symbolic: the menstrual cycle lasts 28 days on average, and the average period lasts 5 days; May 28 is the 28<sup>th</sup> day of the 5<sup>th</sup> month.
Instituée en 2014 par l’organisation à b: Established in 2014 by the German non-profit organization WASH United, the day is supported by bodies such as the United Nations, which encourage collective action so that menstruation does not become an obstacle to education, health or personal development.
Cette journée mondiale vise aussi à sens: The day also aims to raise public awareness of the transformative effects that investments in menstrual health can have on the lives of girls and women. After all, according to UN Women, <l1>more than two billion people around the world menstruate every month</l1>.
‍<strong>Enfin, on ose parler des règles: ‍Finally, we’re daring to talk about periods
Yusle Rodríguez se réjouit de l’ouvertur: Yusle Rodríguez is glad to see growing openness around periods, not least because as a child, she watched her mother suffer terribly every time she was menstruating.
« Pour moi, avoir mes règles, c’était la: “For me, getting my period was the worst thing that could happen to me. My mother suffered so much that I grew up thinking it was something negative, something painful,” she says, as Avril, her daughter, draws and colours while listening closely.
“At home, we never talked about it. So I saw it as an illness,” she adds. Originally from Cuba, Yusle has lived in Montréal for several years.
Donner naissance à une fille l’a poussée: Giving birth to a daughter pushed her to learn more about the menstrual cycle. Today, she talks about it openly as a natural process.
Elle a d’ailleurs participé à plusieurs: She has also attended several of Diana’s workshops with her daughter, and finds in these gatherings a valuable source of information for herself as well, as she begins to feel the first effects of perimenopause.
Diana propose différents types de rencon: Diana offers different types of gatherings. Some are for girls and teens only, without parents present during the information sessions. Others are intergenerational: the young participants are accompanied, usually by their mothers. These sessions cost $30 to $60.
Dans ces espaces, on parle sans détour d: In these spaces, people talk plainly about the vulva, the vagina, the uterus, ovulation, “but also about emotions, changes and self-knowledge,” Diana explains.
Cette approche holistique est celle qui: This holistic approach is what struck Yusle Rodríguez the most.
« Les filles doivent savoir que leur cor: “Girls need to know that their bodies are normal and beautiful (…) The workshop was a blessing, because I saw that my daughter felt safe, that she could talk about this without shame, without fear,” she says.

L’objectif des ateliers, explique Diana,: The goal of the workshops, Diana explains, is to help girls become familiar with the changes their bodies go through at this stage. She chooses her words carefully.
« Ce n’est pas qu’elles deviennent des f: “It’s not that they’re becoming women, as we were so often told in Latin America. They remain girls, and it’s as girls that they need to go through this process. The information is adapted to their age, and it’s essential to respect that.”
De cette manière, les participantes sont: This way, participants are better prepared for their first periods. It’s generally recommended that they have a small kit ready: one they can take everywhere, containing the menstrual products of their choice, a change of clothes, wet wipes and even an herbal tea or infusion, in case they don’t feel well.
Certaines vont même jusqu’à organiser de: Some even go as far as holding menarche ceremonies (the name given to a first period), surrounded by friends and family members.
Ce qui a aussi marqué Yusle, c’est de ré: What also struck Yusle was realizing that, as with her mother, who suffered enormously during her periods (which isn’t the case for her), many period-related symptoms, such as pain, have been normalized over time.
Diana est catégorique : « La douleur, ce: Diana is categorical: “Pain isn’t normal. Neither is heavy bleeding. What’s happened is that we’ve normalized discomfort because the industry just offers us pills so we can keep functioning.”
Lorsque Diana affirme que « la douleur,: When Diana says that “pain isn’t normal,” Claudia Gamboa gently taps the table. Not out of surprise, but to underline the words.
Née en Colombie et écologue de formation: Born in Colombia and trained as an ecologist, Claudia owns the café where our meeting is taking place. She wasn’t the one who went looking for the Happy Periods workshops; rather, they came to her when she met Diana in a women’s circle about food and emotions.
« Ce qu’elle a partagé ce jour-là m’a te: “What she shared that day affected me so much that I told my friends about it. Then I asked her to organize a workshop here, just for us,” she says with a smile.
Claudia avoue qu’elle ne savait presque: Claudia admits she knew almost nothing about her cycle when she got her first period. Today, her periods are regular and not very painful, which she considers a privilege. Yet what struck her most in Diana’s approach is the political and social dimension of the subject.
« Parler de règles, ce n’est pas juste i: “Talking about periods isn’t just personal. It’s also social, it’s political,” she says.
L’atelier a été pour Claudia une prise d: For Claudia, the workshop was a wake-up call: how do women in precarious situations, on the street or in prison, deal with their periods?
« Je n’y avais jamais pensé. Je me suis: “I had never thought about it. I asked myself what kind of world I was living in, to have never put myself in these women’s place,” she says, visibly moved.
Yusle enchaîne : « Même les droits du tr: Yusle chimes in: “Even labour rights don’t take menstruation into account. Before Diana talked about it in a workshop, I had never thought it could be recognized at work. But now, it all makes sense. It should be a right,” she insists.
Diana propose justement que les milieux: Diana, for her part, suggests that workplaces create spaces for care: kits with herbal teas, natural remedies, menstrual products. “Ten women can have their periods in the same office, and none of them talks about it. We’ve normalized working in pain, producing without a break. But that isn’t health,” she says firmly.
La peur d’être perçues comme moins effic: The fear of being seen as less efficient also affects women in perimenopause and menopause. “Many don’t tell their boss, for fear of being judged. It’s a double burden: your body is changing and, on top of that, you have to hide it,” Diana explains.
Si les menstruations sont taboues, la mé: If menstruation is taboo, menopause is a black hole. Many women go through perimenopause without knowing it, attributing their symptoms to depression or anxiety, convinced that they must suffer in silence.
Ce constat a poussé Diana à offrir des a: This observation led Diana to offer workshops for menopausal women. In them, she encourages participants to rest, to exercise, to choose natural foods and to listen to their bodies.
« Si une femme dort mal, a des bouffées: “If a woman is sleeping poorly, having hot flashes, doesn’t understand what’s happening, what she needs first is information. And even that, the health system often doesn’t provide,” she laments.
Juana Rubio est justement à cette étape: Juana Rubio is at precisely this stage of her life. One autumn day, a hot flash surprised her so much that she was frightened. “I spent eight hours sitting at the computer working, sweating. It was a heat that came from inside. I had to open the windows, even though it was cold out,” she says.
Après plusieurs tentatives infructueuses: After several unsuccessful attempts in the public system, the Colombian-born sound artist decided to consult a private clinic specializing in perimenopause.
« La meilleure décision de ma vie ! » af: “The best decision of my life!” she says. There, she got hormone replacement therapy, which eased her hot flashes and her depressive episodes.
Mais ce soulagement a un prix : 250 $ po: But this relief comes at a price: $250 for a first consultation, then $150 for follow-ups. And even though her partner has private insurance she can benefit from, her reimbursement was denied, because the bioidentical hormones she uses are not covered by that insurance plan.
Au Québec, les politiques de rembourseme: In Quebec, reimbursement policies for hormone treatments changed partially in 2022, when the <l1>provincial government announced improved access to two bioidentical hormones</l1>: estradiol-17B in topical gel form and micronized progesterone.
Cependant, ces mesures demeurent incompl: However, these measures remain incomplete, Diana believes. What’s more, many women, like Juana, still struggle to get hormone therapy in the public health network, because of limited access to professionals and the persistent reluctance of many doctors to prescribe this type of therapy.
Comme le montre le cas de Juana, la ques: As Juana’s case shows, the economic question is unavoidable when talking about menstruation or menopause.
Diana souhaite aider ces femmes. C’est p: Diana wants to help these women. That’s why, true to her training in environmental engineering, she also makes and sells reusable cloth sanitary pads, which are somewhat cheaper than the products sold in stores in Montréal.
Justement, ce 28 mai, elle anime un atel: In fact, on May 28, she is leading a pad-making workshop at Claudia’s café. The cost to take part is $30 and includes materials and snacks. A concrete way to move her project forward.

« Les serviettes conventionnelles sont f: “Conventional pads are 90% plastic. They cause odours and irritation. Reusable pads let the skin breathe and change our relationship with blood,” she explains.
Les serviettes que Diana vend sur son si: The pads Diana sells on her website cost $16 each or $27 a pair. Buyers choose the size that best suits their needs and the patterns they like most.
Sur le marché local, un paquet de trois: On the local market, a pack of three eco-pads can cost up to $60. As for period underwear, a well-known Canadian brand sells it at prices ranging from $25 to $48… and you need several pairs to get through a cycle.
Certains arrondissements offrent des <l1: Some boroughs offer <l1>subsidies</l1> for the purchase of reusable menstrual products, but Diana regrets the lack of information about this initiative. Reimbursements vary by borough and range from $50 to $100. Funds are limited, however.
« C’est un processus bureaucratique. Et: “It’s a bureaucratic process. And if you don’t have Internet access or you don’t speak French or English, good luck!” she says. She does her best to inform participants in her workshops, “but it’s still not enough.”
Au cœur du projet Happy Periods, il y a: At the heart of the Happy Periods project is the idea of community, Diana insists.
Les femmes y partagent recettes maison,: Women share homemade recipes, products and experiences there. They support one another in (re)discovering their bodies. Talking about periods or menopause isn’t just an act of health, it’s a healing gesture.
« Si les hommes avaient leurs règles, il: “If men had periods, they’d have paid leave and free products everywhere,” Juana says, laughing. But it’s not a joke. The silence was imposed. Breaking it is a form of justice.
À Montréal, ce changement commence par u: In Montréal, this change begins with a simple question: “What colour is your menstrual blood?”
